iterations.theme: Travel, awareness and responsibility in sales and life: prejudice, active listening, consistency, mistakes and guilt

sections.subtitle: Travel instead of real estate: how the parents invested in their daughters' experiences
sections.screenshot_description: Host Vedran Soric and guest Zoran Salopek in conversation, shot showing the context of the studio recording
sections.content:
The episode begins with a conversation about what guest **Zoran Salopek** gave his daughters in life. Host **Vedran Soric** explains that he and his wife decided to invest in travel instead of real estate and material goods, with the goal of having their daughters experience as many life situations as possible.

The guest comments on this as broadening one's perspective and points out that he did something similar himself. The host states that as a young man he began traveling because his job required it, so his 15 years of work in sales were actually 15 years spent on the road.

Zoran Salopek then describes a turning point in family life. From a sentence said by his daughter, who asked what they would be doing today, he realized that family life had become driven by constant restlessness and the expectation of entertainment. That day he decided that they would not go anywhere and would not do anything, and the family, precisely in this "nothing," found the closeness that, as he says, they had earlier lost in the race for experiences.

sections.subtitle: Balance as the foundation: from awareness to peace at work and at home
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Zoran Salopek speaks about balance, shot with emphasis on the interlocutor in the conversation
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** connects the day of "nothing" with a fundamental life skill, which is the art of stopping. He emphasizes that it is important to know how to stop, both in business and in private and parental life. In his words, one must first learn to start, and then learn to stop.

Zoran Salopek stresses that balance is the key point. Whenever he notices imbalance, he tries to return to the center, both within himself and toward others. Awareness, in his understanding, means noticing the moment in which life begins to drift away from balance.

He develops this view as a theme that runs through the entire conversation: inner peace is not the result of constant action, but of the ability to stop and listen to one's own state.

sections.subtitle: Prejudice is not an assumption: why the difference is crucial in communication and sales
sections.screenshot_description: Host Vedran Soric explains the difference between prejudice and assumption, shot from the studio
sections.content:
Host **Vedran Soric** opens the topic of prejudice and assumptions as two major problems in business, especially in sales. He refers to a LinkedIn post stating that prejudice is much more dangerous than assumption. An assumption, in that sense, is a permissible consideration of a possible outcome, while prejudice represents a conclusion reached in advance.

Guest **Zoran Salopek** explains that prejudice and assumption have the same root. Both come from the inability to admit that one does not know something. He studies terminology in order to understand it, he says, because clarity is key for him, especially when writing books.

The host recalls an experience from training five years ago, when he publicly said "I don't know" for the first time in front of participants. After a short silence he felt relief, which the guest assesses as a sign of maturity and courage, not weakness.

sections.subtitle: Responsibility as personal strength: knowledge with one's own name
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Zoran Salopek emphasizes his own first and last name, graphic display of the word "responsibility" on the screen
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** distinguishes between knowledge and opinion. Knowledge, in his words, carries full responsibility, because a claim is stated under one's own name and surname, without hiding behind other people's authorities, philosophies or courses. Opinion, unlike that, does not carry the same responsibility.

In his experience, business people often remain blocked precisely on this question. He has spoken with serious entrepreneurs whose top ideas failed because they were afraid to speak out under their own name, without the protection of a company or corporation. The guest claims that "the whole universe" functions through responsibility, that is, through the ability of a person to carry their own burden alone.

Host **Vedran Soric** follows up with an example from sales: a salesperson who only collects the invoice has not finished the job, because the collection marks the beginning of new responsibility, which is a repeated purchase. The guest adds that leadership does not happen only in management, but also in the family and in everyday relationships.

sections.subtitle: People ask to get confirmation, not an answer
sections.screenshot_description: Shot of host Vedran Soric considering an example from training, graphic display of questions and answers
sections.content:
The conversation then moves to the question of perception and self-image. Host **Vedran Soric** mentions an example from training in which one participant tried to understand the difference between what a person is really like and how they are perceived. A comparison with a colleague at work or a family member, according to the host, can show the difference between one's own perception and reality.

Guest **Zoran Salopek** raises the question of whether people can accept an answer that does not match their expectations at all. He points out that people often ask in order to get the answer they already have in their heads. Of ten questions he receives, he estimates, eight serve to confirm what people already think, while two are sincere and curious questions.

The host concludes that curiosity is the key trait of a top salesperson, because from it arises the desire to truly help someone understand what they need.

sections.subtitle: Active listening: the silence that reveals the customer's needs
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Zoran Salopek in a moment of pause in the conversation, shot conveying the atmosphere of listening
sections.content:
From curiosity, according to guest **Zoran Salopek**, arises the skill of active listening. Most people, he says, do not listen to the other person, but already prepare an answer in their heads. That is why the first step is to learn to stop talking and truly hear the other person.

Zoran Salopek illustrates this with an example of a salesperson who came to offer him a water-saving system for a hostel. The salesperson talked for a long time and explained excessively, and the guest recognized that a demonstration was missing, so by simply showing it to him, the salesperson sold him the solution. The guest says that the salesperson had actually "sold himself," that is, convinced him through the way he presented himself.

Host **Vedran Soric** explains the notion of the "confused customer": too much explanation on the part of the customer creates a feeling of inferiority and can lead to a decision not to buy the product, not out of need, but out of spite. The guest adds that his silence was intentional, because he wanted to give space to the interlocutor, but the salesperson misinterpreted the silence.

sections.subtitle: Consistency as the foundation of trust: from children's rules to a craftsman who answers the phone
sections.screenshot_description: Graphic showing the words "consistency" and "trust" while the guest talks about rules in the family
sections.content:
The conversation moves to consistency, which guest **Zoran Salopek** describes as one of the key skills. As an example he cites his own parenting: when he says the children may not have chocolate before dinner, that must still hold when they ask a second time. Consistency, in his view, means doing what one says.

The guest also names a criterion by which he chose contractors for his construction projects: it was important to him that craftsmen answer the phone and fulfill what was agreed. Because of such consistency he was willing to accept a higher price, since a consistent person takes responsibility and answers for their work.

Host **Vedran Soric** follows up with the remark that consistency does not exclude the possibility of moving deadlines, but he stresses the importance of communicating this in advance. The guest adds that a consistent person clearly communicates the situation, so one can reach an agreement with them and need not be afraid of their reaction.

sections.subtitle: A mistake as a lesson: the case of faulty brakes and a culture of learning from errors
sections.screenshot_description: Host Vedran Soric talks about his experience with a service center, shot showing a car in a service workshop
sections.content:
Host **Vedran Soric** shares a personal experience with a car. After the brakes were replaced at a service center, a week later he felt the steering wheel shaking. When he returned, it was determined that the front discs had not been replaced. The service center, according to his description, after a call found an error in communication within the chain, and the mechanic's reaction was apologetic, without aggression.

The host stresses that a culture in which mistakes are not hidden, but are openly discussed, is important. As an example he cites military aviation, where every mistake is analyzed down to the smallest detail so that it is not repeated, and he also mentions the Toyota Way in production processes.

Guest **Zoran Salopek** explains the method of examining causes. In his words, one should ask why something happened, then why it happened again, and so on several times, until the cause is reached and not just the consequence. He emphasizes that this method, which he calls the truth, can be simpler than any complex technique.

sections.subtitle: Guilt or responsibility: why excuses are the first automatism
sections.screenshot_description: Graphic comparing the terms "guilt" and "responsibility," guest Zoran Salopek in the conversation
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** claims that the brain is by nature inclined to offer an excuse and justification first. In his view, in the business world the first thing that appears after a mistake is an apology, and such an automatism creates energy that then affects the results. A person who constantly justifies themselves, the guest warns, carries within them an inability to admit their own mistake.

Host **Vedran Soric**, in an example with the head of a sales team, says that a poor result does not necessarily mean that the problem lies in the person. The guest immediately distinguishes the terms: guilt and responsibility are not the same. He states that he is not guilty for all the problems that have arisen, but he is responsible for solving them, just as the owner of a service center is not guilty of an employee's mistake, but answers for resolving it.

Zoran Salopek concludes that the world often revolves around guilt, while responsibility is what brings a solution. He claims that precisely this difference was crucial for his business success.

sections.subtitle: The loneliness of responsibility: why one's life cannot be compared with someone else's
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Zoran Salopek in a conversation about responsibility, shot showing the interlocutors on the studio set
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** describes that only when a person realizes that they alone are responsible for their life, emotions, results and place in society does space open up for maturity. He calls this insight loneliness, but does not understand it negatively, rather as the beginning of independence.

The guest criticizes the tendency to compare. People often talk about how easy it is for someone because they have wealthy parents or an influential family. Host **Vedran Soric** agrees that from the outside we do not see the whole picture. Zoran Salopek points out that it is important not to look for other people's justification, but to ask what we can do with what we have.

As a technique for dealing with such a situation he cites the question "so what?" According to him, it breaks the endless chain of justifications and directs attention to the solution.

sections.subtitle: Ego and apologies: when arrogance comes out
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Zoran Salopek speaks about his own correction, the word "apology" appears on the screen
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** speaks about his own arrogance through an example of when he said something in public that he later had to correct. He describes that he first tried to apologize immediately, but that he published the apology on social media rather than live, which in his opinion showed how burdened he was at that moment by his own image.

Zoran Salopek explains that his ego sometimes "grates on his ears," especially when it comes to apologies. Still, he stresses that the goal is not to be perfect. The goal is to be sufficiently aware and to listen to himself while speaking, because in this way a person can recognize the moment when arrogance has taken over the speech.

Host **Vedran Soric** does not comment in detail on this episode, but steers the conversation toward the question of awareness during speech. The guest concludes that it is enough to listen to one's own words, and even when one catches oneself in an automatism, to recognize it as such.

sections.subtitle: The subconscious and automatisms: why we say what we do not think
sections.screenshot_description: Graphic display of "conscious and subconscious," with the host in the frame listening to the guest
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** speaks about the subconscious and claims that in everyday speech it often surfaces as an automatism. He puts forward the claim that only about five percent is conscious, while noting that this is his view on the topic. He stresses that in speech what is in the head often appears, and a person does not notice it.

He links this topic to beliefs, that is, to what people repeat without thinking. Everyone can check how they speak by listening to themselves in a conversation, not only to their interlocutor.

Host **Vedran Soric** asks whether this can be applied to society as well, that is, whether society as a whole is slowing down because of passive communication through keyboards and audio messages. The guest answers that society as an abstraction does not exist, but that individuals do. In this way he returns to the theme of personal responsibility.

sections.subtitle: Society as an abstraction: responsibility begins with the individual
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Zoran Salopek speaks about responsibility toward society, shot with the title of the book he is writing
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** claims that the notion of "society" is often used to allow an individual to hide behind the collective. In his view, there are no "women" or "salespeople" as abstractions, only concrete persons with their own responsibility. That is why, he says, he constantly emphasizes the theme of responsibility.

The guest states that he is preparing a book whose title, in his words, is "Freedom, Wisdom." In it, he says, generalized advice is deliberately avoided, because what applies to one person is not necessarily applicable to another, due to different perspectives and life circumstances.

Zoran Salopek concludes that it is wise not to make universal judgments about other people's lives, and to take responsibility for one's own contribution to society, beginning with what is within one's own circle.

sections.subtitle: Technology is neither good nor bad: wisdom in its application
sections.screenshot_description: Graphic display of a mobile phone and computer in the context of a conversation about technology, guest Zoran Salopek in the frame
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** speaks about technology as a topic on which people hold different beliefs. For some it is a source of evil, while for others it is a power. In his view, nothing should be rejected or accepted *a priori*, but one should understand why technology exists at all and what place it has in the evolution of society.

As a parent, he says he will not teach his children that technology is bad, but he will not teach them to spend hours in front of a screen either. The goal is to teach them to use it for what they need, to set a boundary, and to move on without it.

Host **Vedran Soric** agrees with this approach and adds that in sales and communication, meaning is often attributed to means. The guest brings this to an example about neutrality: everything in the universe, according to his understanding, is neutral, and people give it meaning through manipulation, theft or cheating.

sections.subtitle: Stolen money and a reaction out of love: an example of a wise response
sections.screenshot_description: Shot with guest Zoran Salopek recounting an incident at the cash register, the cash register visible in the background
sections.content:
As a concrete example, guest **Zoran Salopek** describes a situation in which an employee stole money from the cash register. Another employee informed him about it. Instead of an impulsive reaction, he asked himself what love and truth would do. He concluded that such a reaction would be calm and considered, without haste.

The first step was a question about motive. The guest decided not to assume, but to admit that he did not know the reason, so he confronted the employee with the question of why it had happened. He stresses that he did not focus in advance on punishment, but on understanding the situation and on an opportunity for a way out.

The outcome, according to his description, was the return of the money and the strengthening of trust, but also the development of self-confidence in everyone involved. The guest believes that precisely such a wise reaction is needed by corporations and individuals, including salespeople and managers.

sections.subtitle: Empathy and control of reactions: how to stay calm when it is hardest
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Zoran Salopek in a conversation about empathy, host Vedran Soric in the frame reacting to his story
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** stresses that empathy, compassion and strength do not mean reacting immediately, but staying in wisdom and seeking the truth. When a person does not know what the truth is, he advises asking oneself what one would advise one's own child in the same situation.

As an example he cites a young woman who reported a situation that she knew could cause a major conflict. The guest says that she warned him out of the greatest love, and he promised that he would react wisely and thoughtfully. In the end the friends remained, and the situation was resolved through joint connection.

Host **Vedran Soric** highlights his fascination with the possibility that a person can control their own reaction even in the moment when they react out of love. The guest confirms this, but adds that a person cannot control the outside world, only their own actions and their relationship to themselves.

sections.subtitle: What we can really control: work, consistency and effort, not the result
sections.screenshot_description: Graphic with the words "You have the right to work, you do not have the right to the result," guest Zoran Salopek in the conversation
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** claims that people often want to control what they cannot, such as whether they will be fired, whether others will understand them, or whether a business will succeed. The only control a person has is control over themselves: consistency, reliability and keeping promises.

As a concrete formula he states: "you have the right to work, but you do not have the right to the result." If a person gives everything they have in sales, negotiation or understanding another person, the other side will recognize it, even if the result does not come immediately.

Host **Vedran Soric** adds that it is important to understand what "giving everything" means, because it does not mean that it is the best that can possibly be given, but that it is given in accordance with one's capacity. The guest stresses that it is crucial not to take on someone else's burden.

sections.subtitle: Letting go of what is others': why some salespeople push and others hide
sections.screenshot_description: Graphic display of a team of ten salespeople, guest Zoran Salopek speaks about the division of responsibility
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** explains that when someone on a team pushes too hard, usually someone else somewhere hides. As an example he cites a team of ten salespeople, in which, according to his experience, two try the hardest, six work well, and two hide behind the first two.

Host **Vedran Soric** calls this a statistic, and the guest agrees with it, but stresses that the principle is more important: when one person takes on too much, another withdraws, so responsibility should be returned to the one to whom it belongs.

Zoran Salopek concludes that it is important to let go of things for which a person is not responsible and to stop taking on someone else's burden. This is, in his view, one of the ways in which a healthy division of labor and clarity of roles are created.

sections.subtitle: Leaving the business: lessons that have been exhausted
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Zoran Salopek speaks about the decision to leave the business, shot with a card or depiction of travel
sections.content:
Host **Vedran Soric** asks the guest why he decided to leave the business. Guest **Zoran Salopek** answers that he realized there was nothing more to learn in that business. His lessons, he says, were perseverance, rising out of poverty and help from Caritas, and building businesses from scratch while facing numerous obstacles.

Zoran Salopek says that on that path he learned to listen, to solve problems through understanding and compassion, and not through force. He especially highlighted the moment when he felt that the business no longer gave him what it once had. After 70 countries visited, a friend invited him to go to the 71st, and then he realized that what he had to learn from travel he had already learned.

At the end he says that life nonetheless delayed his departure, so he stayed for two more years in operations, which he interprets as a lesson in patience and the need to leave things in a clean state.

sections.subtitle: Courage for change: leaving the old and entering the unknown
sections.screenshot_description: Guest Zoran Salopek speaks about leaving the company, shot with boxes symbolizing leaving the job
sections.content:
Guest **Zoran Salopek** speaks about how leaving a long-standing job requires strength and the privilege of bringing something to an end. In his words, a person must first clean up behind themselves, settle everything and agree on everything, so that they can turn to a new life without burden.

As an example he cites the day he walked out of his company with boxes in his hands, which, he says, meant that he again had nothing. Still, he was convinced that this was the right path and that everything would be fine. He claims that leaving the old life brings a loss of identity and security, but also entry into the unknown.

Host **Vedran Soric** admits that he too, as an entrepreneur with three companies, sometimes thinks about closing his businesses. He stresses that leaving with unfinished matters would be running away, not a solution, while a clean closing is a sign of maturity.

iterations.theme: Heart and reason, complicating things, self-realization, personal boundaries, change, cycles and the definition of success, and personal freedom

sections.subtitle: Heart or reason: two instances that decide our lives
sections.screenshot_description: Vedran Soric and Zoran Salopek sit at a table in the studio; Salopek gestures while explaining the difference between heart and mind.
sections.content:
The conversation in this part of the episode moves from sales topics to the question of how we make decisions. Guest **Zoran Salopek** claims that in a person there are two instances that mutually take part in deciding: reason and heart. Reason, according to his explanation, serves primarily security. It keeps us in the familiar, in what we already know and what is pleasant to us, so it often perceives the truth as a threat to one's identity. For this reason, at the moment of criticism or confrontation with an unpleasant realization, reason is often activated through defense, justifications and apologies.

The heart, that is, the soul, Salopek describes as the deeper part of a person that knows what is right and shows the way. Reason, in his words, is a friend up to a certain level, while in situations in which criticism must be accepted it becomes an obstacle.

Host **Vedran Soric** follows on the theme of intuition and states that a great deal is said about it in business circles today. As an example he gives his own experience: he always parks exactly where he is going, because he knows in advance that everything will be fine and does not think about whether there will be a space. Salopek accepts this experience as proof of intuition and concludes that both interlocutors understand each other through it, without the need for further explanation.

sections.subtitle: Why we like to complicate simple things
sections.screenshot_description: Shot of the interlocutors in the conversation; Soric asks a question, Salopek leans back and thinks before answering.
sections.content:
Soric asks why people like to complicate things, whether it is because it makes things seem more realistic and important to them. Salopek answers that complication adds importance to what is being discussed. When we present something as complex, others perceive us as more serious and competent, even though the truth often lies in a simple solution.

As an illustration he gives an example of a simple decision: I am going to buy ice cream, not some kind of complex journey. He adds that most problems come down to taking one thing we have gotten stuck on and starting with it. In a humorous tone he says that this is an ordinary decision, like deciding to go eat ćevapi, without any need for complex analysis. In doing so he stresses that things seem difficult to those who do not have enough experience.

Salopek also warns that even excessive ease is not a solution. He describes a conversation with a friend who lived in Brazil, who told him that people there are the opposite of the Balkans: everything must be light, dance and fun, and difficulty is avoided. Such an attitude, according to Salopek, leads to freedom without responsibility. On the other hand, the Balkan habit that everything must be hard is also not correct. Both extremes, he concludes, are wrong.

sections.subtitle: Wisdom as judgment and the ability to choose the right response
sections.screenshot_description: Salopek in conversation with the host, in medium shot, while speaking about wisdom and black-and-white thinking.
sections.content:
Soric introduces the topic of black-and-white thinking and asks whether it is appropriate to always look for a solution or to focus on problems. Salopek answers that situations do not allow simple categories. Wisdom, in his understanding, is the ability to know when to accept and when to change, when to apologize, when to attack and when to withdraw, and when to act. Black-and-white thinking does not lead to a wise answer.

The host then asks about Salopek's education. The guest states that he finished secondary agricultural school, a program in animal husbandry. Soric asks whether he had previously been acquainted with psychology or philosophy, to which Salopek answers negatively. Soric recalls that in secondary school philosophy was unclear to him and that he only began to understand it later.

Salopek concludes that it is necessary to be a whole person. This means integrating so-called feminine skills, such as acceptance, relaxation and forgiveness, with so-called masculine skills, such as confrontation, determination and responsibility. Only when a person can be capable of both do they have a choice in how they will react in a given situation. Asked what he would call the hardest conversation of his life, the guest answers that it was the conversation with himself at the age of nineteen, during a difficult period marked by poverty, family violence and a feeling of loneliness. At that time he realized that part of the problem was with him and that it was his responsibility to initiate change.

sections.subtitle: Self-realization begins by turning focus toward oneself
sections.screenshot_description: Soric listens to the guest, who leans forward and points toward himself while speaking about getting to know oneself.
sections.content:
Salopek claims that the goal of life is to get to know oneself. He describes self-realization as a process that unfolds over the whole of life and that begins at the point when a person stops looking for someone to blame in the outside world. As an indicator of not knowing oneself, he cites the reaction to other people's words: if someone's remark sets us off, it means we do not yet know how we function.

The host asks whether that was precisely the moment in which Salopek began to get to know himself, to which the guest answers affirmatively. He describes that at that time he stepped into a new phase, like a student entering school. Instead of saying "you are all to blame," he began to ask what in this was up to him. That process, he explains, means turning the focus from the outside world to oneself.

Salopek states that since then, in every situation, he looks at what he should learn from it. He considers such an approach the foundation of personal growth and a prerequisite for a deeper understanding of one's own reactions, beliefs and patterns.

sections.subtitle: Taking responsibility for one's own life
sections.screenshot_description: Graphic display or shot of Salopek as he emphasizes the concept of responsibility, while the host listens to him with a faint smile.
sections.content:
Salopek distinguishes guilt from responsibility. He explains that a person can be innocent of a particular problem, but still be responsible for solving it. As an example he cites the owner of a service center who did not cause the employee's mistake, but who nonetheless takes responsibility and calls the customer with a promise that the problem will be resolved. His conclusion is that guilt is something that happened, while responsibility is what follows.

Soric follows with a parallel from sales management, in which the head of a team often concludes that the problem lies with a weak performer, while responsibility may also lie with the team leader. Salopek confirms that this is an important difference and states that this is precisely the reason he succeeded in the business world: he did not look at who was guilty, but at whose responsibility it was to solve the problem.

The guest stresses that many people compare themselves with others, pointing to other people's advantages such as wealthy parents or connections in the business world. However, such a comparison ignores the fact that we do not see the whole picture of someone else's life. Responsibility for one's own life, emotions, results and position in society remains with the individual, regardless of the starting point. Salopek calls this loneliness, but in the sense of independence and inner strength.

sections.subtitle: Personal boundaries, compensation and the importance of consistency
sections.screenshot_description: Shot in which Salopek explains the principle of compensation, while Soric sits thoughtfully and listens.
sections.content:
The conversation then turns to personal boundaries and compromises. Salopek stresses that the ability to reach agreement is key in business, private and family life, but that to agree one must know one's own boundaries. Most people, in his view, know how to set boundaries toward others, but do not ask how they set boundaries toward themselves, that is, how they avoid overburdening others and themselves.

As an explanation for why people break other people's boundaries while not protecting their own, the guest cites the principle of compensation. A person who carries dissatisfaction or some weakness within is often compelled to make up for it by reacting toward the outside world, and sometimes this grows into pride. Soric describes people who occasionally flare up, lash out at everyone and then disappear, while consistency is what is decisive. Salopek sums this up with the claim that everything that goes up must come down, so it is important to maintain stability.

Soric recalls that he recently wrote that the best salespeople are often boring, because they are consistent and reliable. Salopek confirms this and adds that his own life today is considerably calmer and less exciting than before, but that precisely such stability is a sign of inner balance.

sections.subtitle: When it is wise to make a change and when to keep what exists
sections.screenshot_description: Soric and Salopek in a lively conversation; Soric gestures with his hands while describing reorganizations in companies.
sections.content:
Salopek claims that change is inevitable and that a person has only one right: to choose whether they will initiate it themselves or whether it will be imposed on them. Soric follows with the observation that change is the only constant. Salopek then talks about corporations that often change systems without real need, so that after a few years they return to old solutions. Such changes, in his view, do not arise from wisdom but from a desire to show activity and importance.

Soric ironically notes that in corporate language a change is often renamed as restructuring, and Salopek adds that sometimes it is great wisdom and strength to keep things as they are. Wisdom does not necessarily mean changing, but knowing when a change is useful. Soric gives an example from the European automotive industry which, in his assessment, tried to change its business in a way that was not fully thought through.

Salopek concludes that wisdom is in fact a judgment based on experience. It makes it possible to decide better whether something should be changed or not.

sections.subtitle: Life cycles, greed and long-term planning
sections.screenshot_description: Chart or visual display of cycles of growth and decline, while Salopek explains the cycles of the economy in the background.
sections.content:
Soric asks whether numbers can explain everything, and Salopek answers that peace, joy and satisfaction cannot be expressed in numbers. He recalls that in history there was too little information, while today the situation is reversed: there is too much information. That is why wisdom now lies in knowing what is needed and stopping in time. "Enough" is, in his words, a sign of wisdom. Enough satisfaction, pleasures and money.

Salopek claims that greed is one of the causes of inflation, and explains that everything in the universe, including the economy, functions in cycles. He recalls the biblical story of the seven fat and seven lean cows and stresses that after a rise there always comes a fall.

As a personal example he states that in the first year of running the hostel he earned a lot, but stopped and thought. He decided not to spend everything, but to save. The following year the borders were closed, there were no tourists, and the hostel remained empty. The savings, according to him, allowed him to survive the following winters. He concludes that long-term planning is necessary for stability, both emotional and financial.

He then describes a client from Serbia, a chocolate manufacturer, who spent an hour with him looking for the cause of a stall in the business. It turned out that the problem was not technical in nature, but emotional. Salopek uses this as an illustration that business problems often come down to human and family matters.

sections.subtitle: Definition of success: the result is a consequence, and work is valuable in itself
sections.screenshot_description: Salopek smiles and calmly speaks about his hostel and neighborhood in Zagreb, while Soric listens and takes notes.
sections.content:
Salopek describes his approach to business through the example of a hostel in Zagreb. He was the first to open a facility in a neighborhood that was then neglected, and after him came a restaurant and a hair salon. Today the neighborhood, in his words, looks considerably better. His motivation was not primarily earnings, but creating, employing people, hosting guests from all over the world and presenting a city he loves. Money, he says, was a consequence, not a goal.

Soric recalls his experience with debtors and says that in his company he rarely went to court proceedings, but instead talked with people. In one case a debtor got in touch after a long time with an apology and a promise that he had not forgotten. Such experiences, in his view, confirm that the decision to remain honest was correct.

Salopek concludes that it is more important to look at what is right to do than at what will be gained. A person has the right to work, but has no right to a specific result. Such thinking, in his view, frees one from pressure and makes peace and joy possible.

sections.subtitle: Freedom as the common denominator of happiness, peace and fulfillment
sections.screenshot_description: Close-up of Salopek as he says the words "freedom" and "success is an illusion"; Soric is also visible in the frame, writing down key terms.
sections.content:
Salopek claims that peace, joy, satisfaction and fulfillment have a common denominator, and that is freedom. He distinguishes personal, emotional, financial and physical freedom. Freedom, in his view, lies in balance. A person must be strong enough and aware enough that nothing disturbs their inner balance, that is, that they do not allow everything to happen "inside them." This requires a great deal of experience.

He then puts forward the thesis that success is an illusion. He explains that after a goal has been reached, the feeling that it is unimportant appears very quickly. As an example he cites finishing university, after which a new question appears, such as looking for a job. The story of a man who bought a 40-meter yacht in order to find peace, but who nonetheless realized that it did not bring him lasting satisfaction, illustrates that success and material goods cannot be substituted for inner peace.

Soric asks whether the new definition of success for the guest is precisely that joy and fulfillment. Salopek stresses that everyone has their own definition of success, and that what is common to everyone is that success becomes unimportant over time. Soric concludes that success cannot be quantified, to which Salopek answers that the personal experience must be lived in order to understand its transience.

Salopek finally says that everything can be summed up in one thought: it is not important what you do, but why. If one acts from strength and not from weakness, life is directed toward freedom. The conversation ends with an announcement of the next episode.
